The First Page

December 1909
The Wager Ledger
An illustrated edition · Complete original story

"You have walked up from the village, Doctor, because the fly was taken, and you have done it in your town boots. I am sorry for both. There is a parcel on the table which has been sorry for itself since noon."

Mr. Sherlock Holmes had by that time retired from London to a small farm upon the downs, five miles from Eastbourne, where he divided his days between study and the keeping of bees. The doctor came to him for an occasional week-end, and on the afternoon of Friday, the seventeenth of December, 1909, a bitterly cold one, he came upon his friend standing bareheaded in the orchard among the hives, which were packed for the season with sacking and straw, and each with its little door closed to the width of two fingers.

"They ask nothing of me until February," said Holmes, as they went indoors. "It is the only fault that I find in them."

The parcel lay under the lamp. It was square and heavy, done up in brown paper which had evidently served before, tied with tape in both directions, and sealed at every knot. It had not been opened.

"You have not looked inside?" said the doctor.

"No need. The sender is an elderly man who was once in the police. He is ill, and addressed it in bed. He is poor. And he does not expect to want the contents again."

"My dear Holmes!"

"It is simple enough, and no more remarkable than any other conclusion when the steps are taken in order. Observe the knots. That is a slip-knot of a very particular kind, drawn so that a second person cannot loosen it without leaving a trace, and I have seen it on a hundred bundles of evidence at Bow Street. It is evidence in itself, for a constable learns it in his first year and never ties any other. Each knot is sealed, which is habit again; but the wax is the end of a candle, which is not. Look next at the address. The lines climb from left to right, and the downstrokes have gone through the paper in two places, as they do when a man writes upon his knee with a blanket under it."

"And the poverty?"

"There is a more suggestive fact. The parcel is registered. The fee and the postage are made up entirely of halfpenny stamps, and no two of them were torn from the same sheet. They were bought one at a time, Doctor, as a man buys them who has money on one day of the week and counts it for the other six."

"But why should he not want the things again?"

"Because he has not troubled to write his name outside for their return, and a man who expects to see a thing again does not send the only copy of it by post without that precaution." He cut the tape above the first seal, leaving the knots entire, and unfolded a sheet of ruled paper which lay uppermost. "I have not been paid for much of late. Let us see what he offers."

He read it aloud, standing by the fire.

Lambeth, 16 Dec. 1909.

Mr. Holmes,—You were dead once and I swore to it. I am the other party now, and the doctors will swear to me by Christmas.

Herewith my file on P. Fogg, thirty-seven years, complete but for one line. The Sunday Argus prints the first of me on Sunday. It goes to press on Saturday at six.

There is a paper in their proof that is not in my file. I have not told them so. Read both. Then do what you like. I shall not lift a hand either way.

I cannot pay you. The file is the fee.

I do not read the doctor. Give him my compliments.

"The impudence of the man!" said the doctor warmly. "Is that the creature who swore he had seen you in the river?"

"The same. He is also the creature who followed Mr. Fogg round the world upon a description and a likeness, and was knocked down at the end of it. Pray help me to lay these things out."

The inventory was a curious one. There were thirty-seven black notebooks, one for each year, every one tied with the same tape. There was a bundle of older papers, which contained a telegram on a faded pink form, with a round stamp that read LIVERPOOL, DE 20 72; a copy, in a clerk's writing, of the proceedings of an inquiry held in 1861; and eleven printed lists of subscriptions to a society for the relief of shipwrecked fishermen and mariners. The last article was of a different character from all the rest. It was a long slip of printer's proof, still limp, and smelling strongly of ink, and across the head of it ran the words ROUND THE WORLD AFTER THE WRONG MAN, AND THE RIGHT ONE.

"That did not come out of any old man's cupboard," said the doctor.

"No. It is the one wrong thing upon the table, and it is the reason for all the others." Holmes glanced at the clock. "It is past four. He has given me one working day. I remember a lady who did the same."

"He says that the file is complete but for one line. Which line?"

"The one that I have not been paid for since 1887," said Holmes, and drew his chair to the table.

They read until long after the housekeeper had gone to bed, Holmes taking the notebooks in their order and the doctor the printed slip, while the frost thickened upon the panes.

"Here is the heart of it," said the doctor at last. "I will give it you as it stands. It says that in December 1860 Mr. Fogg, being then eight-and-twenty years of age, was master of a barque, the Sarah Pellew, homeward from Calcutta; that he put her upon the rocks of Scilly in the dead of the night, through an error in his reckoning; and that nineteen persons were drowned, of whom one was his elder brother. Can that be true?"

"The inquiry puts it beyond all reasonable doubt. It is a dreadful business, but it is a fact. What more?"

"A great deal more. It says that when he was arrested at Liverpool in 1872 he was released too soon, and that a telegram arrived after he had gone. Here it is, set out in a box by itself."

POST OFFICE TELEGRAPHS.

From Scotland Yard, London. To Inspector —, Custom House, Liverpool.

Received at 4.10 p.m. Dated stamp: LIVERPOOL, DE 21 72.

Strand states had confederate in passage of notes. Description answers Fogg. Hold him.

"And the moral of it?"

"That the Bank had got back its notes, that great persons in a great club took an interest, and that the matter was allowed to sleep. There is a line in capitals about one law for Pall Mall."

"They could not have chosen a better week for it. What do you make of the notebooks, Doctor? Take the last of them, and look at it as a medical man."

The doctor held the last book under the lamp and turned the leaves slowly, from the new year to the Wednesday of that very week, where the writing stopped.

"It is a failing heart, Holmes, and I should say that death is not far off. The signs are perfectly clear. See how the hand drops at the end of each line, and the words crowd one another. These later pages were written by a man propped up, who had to rest between sentences. I should give him a fortnight."

"One for you, Doctor. He gave himself until Christmas."

"There is another thing, though it is not medicine. The early books are a case. He is building it: names, dates, a witness here and a cabman there. But after the spring of 'ninety-four there is nothing to build. 'Left at half past eleven. Five hundred and seventy-five paces. Home at midnight.' Page after page of it! It is a case-book, Holmes, with no case in it."

Holmes laid down his pipe and regarded his friend with real attention.

"That is admirably observed, and the inference is a sound one. It is no longer a case; it is a watch which he has kept. I have known one other man who kept such a watch upon a friend, and he sold it to the Strand."

The doctor coloured, and returned in some haste to the oldest of the books, and it was there, upon the page which dealt with Liverpool, that he came upon a thing which puzzled him. The entry was written in black ink, faded to brown: Sat. 21 Dec. Liverpool Custom House. Took him 11.40. Loosed him 2.33. Beside it in the margin, in red ink which was still perfectly bright, and in a much later hand, stood the words Fri. 20th. He says. 5 Apr. 94.

"What does he mean by that? It is a very curious addition."

"What day of the week," said Holmes, "was the twenty-first of December, 1872?"

"A Saturday. Every account says so. It says so here."

"Yes," said Holmes. "Every account says so."

He would add nothing to this remark, but took up the notebook of 1901, found the month of March with very little search, and read out a single entry.

"'25 March. A lady, 11h 20m, by cab, with luggage. Stayed.'" He was silent for some moments, and then he drew towards him one of the printed lists of the seamen's charity, ran his long finger down the column of sums, and appeared to be counting something, which he did not name. "We shall go up by the first train," said he. "You had better sleep, Doctor. I shall not."

The house was one of a long, soot-coloured row which opened off the Kennington Road, and the room was at the back of the second floor, a very clean, bare room, containing an iron bed, a table, a single chair, and a large deal box which stood open and empty against the wall. Holmes set down beside it the bag in which he had carried the notebooks. A little book in a buff cover lay upon the mantelpiece, and he glanced at it as he took off his gloves.

"He has not left this room since Friday week," said he to the landlady.

"Lord, sir, who told you that?"

"His pension book suggested it. There are two orders in it which have not been cut, and I do not think that he is a man to leave ten shillings lying at a post office."

The man in the bed was small and slight, and lay propped upon three pillows, with his lips blue and his hands outside the quilt. His eyebrows, which in former years had gone up and down continually without his leave, were now perfectly still, and it was the doctor's opinion that this alteration told more than the colour of his lips.

"You came," said he. "I told myself that you would come for the same reason that took me to Meiringen. You can't leave a thing unseen. Put your doctor in the chair. No, leave his hand off my wrist; I know what he'll find. Have you read it?"

"All of it. I should like to hear it from you."

"You'll hear it, then, for I've not told it to a living soul, and I have had it by heart a long while. In 'seventy-two I followed him on a description and a likeness. I followed him to Suez and Bombay, to Hong Kong and Yokohama, and across the Americas, and I was sure of him at every port, because a man who spends bank-notes like that is either a thief or a lunatic, and he did not look like a lunatic. Then we came to New York and missed the Liverpool boat, and I thought the game was finished. It wasn't. He got aboard a trading steamer called the Henrietta that was bound for Bordeaux, and in a day and a half he had the crew in his pocket and the captain locked in the cabin, and he was taking her to Liverpool himself."

He stopped for breath, and the doctor held a cup to his mouth.

"When the coal gave out he bought the ship from under the man's feet, and he fed her own deckhouses and bulwarks into her furnaces until she was a hull with a funnel on it. I stood on that deck, Mr. Holmes, with the spray coming over, and I watched him. He took her across like a man putting on his own coat. He gave his orders before the weather changed, not after it. He never looked to see if they were obeyed. And I knew two things for certain before we raised the Irish coast: that he was no bank thief, and that he had been a ship's master. It was the most extraordinary thing that I ever saw done, and it frightened me. I knew the truth of him then. It was of no use to me. I had a warrant in my pocket and my name upon it, and I served it at Liverpool just the same."

"And afterwards you made use of your second fact."

"Afterwards I had leisure. They had me on the carpet at Scotland Yard the very next afternoon after I got to town, for the Yard did not care to keep an officer who had arrested an innocent man in the sight of all England, and by the spring of 'seventy-three I was my own master. I went to the Custom House in London, where they keep the registers of the merchant officers, and I found him in a single morning. Certificate at four-and-twenty. A command at eight-and-twenty. The Sarah Pellew, four hundred and twenty tons, with his elder brother aboard her as owner. Six days of thick weather coming up to the Channel, with no sight of sun or star, and a hard frost on top of it. He had his chronometer and he trusted it, and it was four minutes wrong. At a quarter past two in the morning, she struck on the Western Rocks. There were one-and-thirty souls in her. Twelve were got off. The brother was not one, and they never found him. There was an inquiry, and they found for the master, and he never went to sea again."

For some moments there was no sound in the room but the old man's laboured breathing.

"Do you mark the date?" said he. "The twenty-first of December, 1860. Twelve years after it, to the day as he reckoned the day, he was out again in his figures, by a whole four-and-twenty hours this time, and it made his fortune over again and got him a wife. Some men's errors are paid for by other people. Mine was. His first one was. His second was paid to him in gold."

"There are the printed lists," said Holmes.

"Ah! You've been at those. Any man who has seen that betting-book wants to know why he writes it, and I saw it lying open on his desk in April of 'ninety-four, with my own hat beside it, and the words One sovereign at the foot of the page. The same morning, in Cornhill, I heard him read out of it the word Lost. Every year the seamen's society prints the names of those who give. Every year there is one gift with no name to it, only the words 'A Master.' Never the same sum twice. Forty-one pounds. Twenty-nine. Fifty-three. I could not make head or tail of it until that morning. Then I saw it. It is one sovereign for each time that he has been wrong. He fines himself, Mr. Holmes, and he pays the fine to the drowned."

The doctor turned abruptly towards the window. Holmes did not move.

"Pray continue. After the spring of 'ninety-four?"

"After that I had no case. I had given him my word in a manner of speaking, and there was my confession lying in a safe in Cornhill. I kept on. I told myself that I was waiting for the day when he would be late." There was a long pause. "He never was."

"And the newspaper?"

"Forty guineas, to be paid in two parts, and I have had ten. I lent them the first notebook, the one of the journey, and no other. They had it nine weeks. On Tuesday they sent me their proof, to show how handsomely it would look, and there in the middle of it was a telegram. I never had it. I never heard of it. I was not asked. If I had had that paper in my hand at Liverpool, he would never have left the Custom House."

"You have not told them so."

"No." The old man raised himself upon one elbow, and a dull flush came into his face. "With that telegram I was right! Do you see it? For one Sunday, in a million houses, I was right in 'seventy-two, and the Yard was wrong to break me, and the great gentlemen hushed it up. I need only hold my tongue. And I should be dead before ever I could be found out. Who would be hurt but a man of seven-and-seventy who has never in his life gone to law? I have lain two days looking at that slip of paper. Then I tied up the books."

"Why did you send them to me?"

"Because you've never been wrong about anything, they tell me, and I wanted to see what such a man does with it."

"I have been wrong often enough. You leave the wreck to stand?"

"It's accurate."

"That is what he will say."

"Then ask him. I never heard him say anything else." He sank back; but as Holmes took up his hat the pale eyes opened once more. "The one line, Mr. Holmes. I have what he does. I have had it to the minute for seven-and-thirty years. What is it for?"

"Before we carry this inquiry any further," said Holmes in the cab, "I wish to have it read by a seaman."

They found one at a shipping office near the Tower, a long, low room with a stove at one end of it, where two young clerks were making a show of attending to their ledgers while an elderly master mariner talked to them from a bench. He was lean and sunburnt, with sunken cheeks and a yellow tinge in them, and he sat bolt upright with his arms dropped and the palms of his hands turned outwards, so that he resembled some idol which had been set down there to await shipment. He was in the middle of a sentence which the clerks had very evidently heard before. He broke it off without resentment when Holmes laid the paper before him.

"You were brought up in sail," said Holmes, "you have lately commanded in steam, and a great part of your life has been passed in the East. The ridges across your palms were made by rope, there is coal worked into the cracks of them, and that yellow was never got in the Channel."

"And you keep bees," said the mariner placidly. "There's wax under your nails."

Holmes laughed so heartily that both the clerks looked up. The seaman, who had not smiled, read the inquiry through from the first page to the last, turned back to the evidence of the second mate, and read that again.

"Four minutes of time," said he, "is one degree of longitude. You understand that? The sun goes round, and your box tells you what o'clock it is at Greenwich while he is doing it, and the difference is where you are. Off Scilly a degree is some eight-and-thirty miles. This man thought the Bishop light was eight-and-thirty miles from where it stood. He had had six days of it without a sight, and frost on top. I have seen a good chronometer go ten seconds a day in a cold snap, and never a word of warning."

"Was it his fault?"

"The court said not. That is not the question you mean. A man may be cleared by every assessor in London and know very well that it was his hand pricked off the position. I knew one who lost his certificate at an inquiry out East. He was the other sort. He jumped." He contemplated the stove for some moments. "Did this one keep a rate afterwards?"

"A what?"

"A rate. Every day you set your box against the true time, and you write down what she has gained or lost. You write it whether it pleases you or not, for it is the only way to know how far to trust her to-morrow. It is the last thing a master leaves off. I have known them keep it in their gardens, with nothing to navigate but the road to the public-house."

Holmes said nothing whatever. The doctor had known him for more than half his life, and he looked at him, and then looked quickly away again.

"He counts his paces," said the doctor.

"Of course he does. It is all that the land gives a man for a log-line." The mariner handed back the paper. "He was one of us," said he gravely, and resumed his story at the very word where he had left it. "Pass the ink, will you."

"Monsieur Holmes!" cried the steward, as he opened the door of No. 7, Savile Row. "And the doctor, who writes down Monsieur Holmes! Come in, come in out of the cold. He is at home until half past eleven."

He was seven-and-sixty, as round and as pink as ever. It wanted some twenty minutes of the half-hour when they were shown into the study. Mr. Fogg rose to receive them, white-haired and perfectly upright in his seven-and-seventieth year, with his watch open in his hand.

"I can give you—"

"He can give you until luncheon, Mr. Holmes," said the lady from her chair by the fire. "I have altered that."

She was small and dark and held herself as straight as her husband, and there was a look of quiet amusement upon her fine face which the doctor had not seen there when he last beheld it, at a railway carriage door. Mr. Fogg considered her for a moment, closed his watch, but did not put it away. Holmes laid upon the desk the copy of the inquiry and the printer's slip. The old gentleman took up the first and was master of it, as it seemed, in about four seconds.

"Is it accurate?" said Holmes.

"No. It was four minutes and eleven seconds."

For a space no one spoke. The doctor looked at the lady. She had not raised her eyes from the fire, and there was no surprise whatever in her face.

"The Sunday Argus means to print it," said Holmes, "to a million readers, to-morrow morning."

"If it is corrected, I can have no objection to it."

"And this?"

Mr. Fogg read the telegram in its box, and for the first time a slight line appeared between his brows.

"I was not at Liverpool on the twenty-first."

"Every account says that you were."

"Every account is a day out. So was I."

He drew from his pocket the small green book, and he did what Holmes, who had seen him consult it upon four occasions, had never yet seen him do. He opened it at the first page, and turned it round upon the desk. There was a single entry, in a firm, square writing.

Sat. 21 Dec. 1872. Liverpool, 11h 40m a.m. 80th day.

Nothing stood beneath it. It had never been corrected.

"I should be obliged for the times which followed," said Holmes.

Mr. Fogg gave them without looking at the book.

"Released at two thirty-three. The special at three. London at ten minutes to nine. I was five minutes late. The next evening I was three seconds early."

"May I have a copy of the page?"

"The ledger is not lent. It will be in Fleet Street by five."

Holmes had been turning over the later leaves with a light hand, and he paused. The lady, who had evidently observed where he paused, leaned forward from her chair.

"He lost his sovereign, Mr. Holmes," said she. "He had wagered that I should come before the day, and I came upon it. I have told him that it was very careless of me."

25 Dec. 1900. Cheque 109. £250. By hand, 8h 10m. That she will return before Lady Day. One sovereign.

Lost. 25 March, 11h 20m.

"But that is the very hour in the old man's book!" cried the doctor, who had read it the night before. "The two agree to the minute."

"You had better come with us to Fleet Street," said Holmes. "It is your name which they propose to blacken."

"A statement that is false will be found to be false. I have not been to law in my life."

Holmes bowed and moved to the door. With his hand upon it he stopped, and spoke in a lower tone than was usual with him.

"In 'ninety-one, Mr. Fogg, you would not give me up for drowned, when there was no body. I think that I know now whom you were looking for."

Mr. Fogg looked at his watch. He looked at it for a long while, and he did not say what it told him.

The lady came out with them into the hall, and drew the study door close behind her.

"Where does the old man lie?" she asked. Holmes wrote the address upon one of his cards, and she took it. "I may be asked," said she. "I have found of late that it is possible."

The office of the Sunday Argus stood in a narrow court off Fleet Street, and at ten minutes past five upon that Saturday it was a place of uproar. Gas and electric light burned together upon the stairs, where a yellow poster demanded of all who climbed them whether it was to be PEERS OR PEOPLE; boys ran up and down with wet slips in their fists; and the whole building trembled from the cellars upwards as the great machines were warmed for the night. The editor received his visitors in an inner room. He was a well-dressed man of two-and-fifty, quick, fresh-coloured and agreeable, with a tired look about the eyes, and he came round his table with both hands extended.

"Mr. Sherlock Holmes! You are worth a column to me merely by walking up my stairs. Sit down. This is Mr. Quarmby, our solicitor, who is here because my proprietor is nervous this month. And this is your friend the doctor, whose work I have long envied for its sales."

Mr. Quarmby was a dry, grey, careful person of sixty, who rose an inch from his chair and sank back again.

"I have come about your first chapter," said Holmes. "I am sorry to say that it cannot be printed as it stands."

"Cannot!" The editor smiled indulgently. "You have been out of London some years, Mr. Holmes. Things move. I understand that you keep bees."

"They keep me."

"Very good; I shall use that. But let me put you in possession of the situation, for I like a man to know where he stands before he quarrels with me. Print is a trade. I said so when I was five-and-twenty and was thought cynical, and I learned it afterwards upon a monthly, in the eighties, where we starved genteelly for the sake of literature. My wife's first husband wrote novels that nobody bought. I resolved to print what somebody would. Now, what does the public wish to read this week? It wishes to read that the clubs are rotten, and that there is one law for the man who walks to them and another for the man who sweeps their steps. I do not make the appetite. I am merely paid to feed it. Your old gentleman is a windfall such as comes once in a man's career: a detective who was wrong, with a grudge which has kept sweet for thirty-seven years, and a dying man into the bargain. The telegram came to me with the rest. I should be a fool to leave it out, and my proprietor does not pay me to be a fool."

"Came to you from whom?"

"With the rest, Mr. Holmes."

"They told us in the court below, when we asked our way," said the doctor drily, "that you were a man of your day, whatever the day might be."

"You write very little yourself now, I perceive," said Holmes pleasantly, "but you corrected this chapter with your own hand."

The editor's eyebrows rose. "Now how the deuce do you get at that?"

"A man who is much at his desk with a pen carries the mark of it upon his right cuff, and yours is spotless. But there is a green pencil in your waistcoat pocket, of which the point has lately been used, and the corrections upon the old man's proof are in green. You did not leave him to a sub-editor. You have a regard for this chapter."

"I have the highest regard for it."

"Then you will not object to a small test. Would you have your foreman come in, and read aloud to us the telegram precisely as it will stand in a million copies, with the stamp and the hour?"

The editor shrugged his shoulders, touched a bell, and in a moment a large man in a leather apron stood in the doorway, wiping his fingers. He took the slip, held it at the length of his arm, and read it out in a loud, flat voice, as one who has no interest in the sense of what passes through his hands.

"'Liverpool, December the twenty-first, 'seventy-two. Received at ten minutes past four.'"

"Thank you. You will note the day, Mr. Quarmby," said Holmes. "The paper stands upon it?"

"It stands upon the Post Office," said the editor.

"Very well. I must ask for your patience while I explain a point which is perfectly simple, and which has been before the eyes of the whole world since 1872. Every printed account declares that Mr. Fogg was arrested at Liverpool on Saturday, the twenty-first. The old man's own notebook says so. His prisoner's diary says so. Each of them believed it. Now consider the facts which followed. Mr. Fogg was released at twenty-seven minutes before three. He could not get a special train until three o'clock, and he reached London at ten minutes before nine. His wager required him to be in the saloon of the Reform Club at a quarter before nine. Upon that day, therefore, he was five minutes late, and he had lost it."

"But, Holmes," cried the doctor, who could not contain himself, "he did win! All the world knows that he won."

"Precisely, Doctor. You have put your finger upon the only fact that matters. He stood in the saloon of the Reform Club at a quarter before nine on the evening of Saturday, the twenty-first of December, in the presence of five gentlemen who had every reason to wish him elsewhere, and he collected twenty thousand pounds. Now a man cannot be five minutes too late upon a Saturday and win upon the evening of the same Saturday. One of those two days is not a Saturday. There is no room for doubt which it is, for the five gentlemen had their calendars and their newspapers, whereas the traveller had only his diary. He had gone round the world towards the east, meeting every sunrise a little before it was due, and in the whole circuit he had gained a day without knowing it. So had the officer who pursued him. The conclusion is unavoidable. The day at Liverpool was therefore Friday, the twentieth."

Mr. Quarmby had taken out a pencil. The editor was no longer smiling, but he did not appear to be alarmed.

"Ingenious," said he. "But consider my position, Mr. Holmes. You bring me a piece of arithmetic. My readers do not buy arithmetic. I have a printed form with a Post Office stamp upon it, which a man can see and understand; and you have a gentleman travelling round the globe and mislaying a day in his luggage. Which do you suppose they will believe over their breakfast? If the old man was a day out, why should not the clerk at Liverpool have been a day out also, or his stamp wrongly set? I cannot be expected to pull my best chapter to pieces upon a theory."

"The clerk had not been to sea, and it is impossible that his stamp should have differed from every almanac in the town for a whole day unobserved. But you ask for evidence, and you are right to ask for it." Holmes drew from his pocket-book the faded pink form and laid it upon the table beside the printed slip. "Here is the telegram which the officer did receive, and upon which he opened the door. 'Strand arrested Edinburgh 17th. Release Fogg.' Be good enough to read the stamp, Mr. Quarmby."

"Liverpool," said the solicitor slowly. "December the twentieth."

"The Post Office, you see, had not been round the world."

At this moment there was a commotion upon the stairs, the glass door was thrown open, and the steward appeared, extremely out of breath, with his hat in one hand and a long envelope in the other.

"Five o'clock, monsieur said," said he, panting, "and it is twenty minutes after, because of all these persons in the Strand. Never has such a thing happened to me!"

Mr. Quarmby opened the envelope, read the single line which it contained, and read it a second time aloud.

"'Sat. 21 Dec. 1872. Liverpool.' Why, this supports the paper, Mr. Holmes! Here is the man himself, and he says Saturday."

"He says what he believed when he wrote it. Turn up the Times of Monday, the twenty-third, which I have no doubt that you can do in this building, and satisfy yourself upon what evening he walked into his club. Then consider your two telegrams. If the twentieth was the day of his arrest, he was in London by that night, and on the Saturday afternoon he was sitting quietly in his own house in Savile Row, while the officer, as he tells me, was being reprimanded at Scotland Yard. Yet your form is sent from Scotland Yard to that officer at Liverpool, and orders him to hold a man who is two hundred miles away from him. And if you will have it that the twenty-first was the day at Liverpool after all, then Mr. Fogg could not have reached London before ten minutes to nine, and he never won his wager, and the whole kingdom has been mistaken for seven-and-thirty years. You may print one or the other. I do not see how you can print both."

The solicitor's lips moved. He was evidently working the sum for himself, from three o'clock to ten minutes before nine, and from ten minutes before nine to a quarter before it. At the end of it he took the printed slip, drew his pen very deliberately across the box from one corner to the other, and handed it back to the editor.

"It must be so," said Mr. Quarmby, half to himself. "The fact is that one of these two papers is impossible, and it is not the one with the evidence behind it. Not upon my advice. Nor upon anybody's."

"Well," said the editor, after a moment, "somebody has been exceedingly clumsy. I suppose you will say that it was the old man."

"On the contrary, he is certainly the one person who could not possibly have done it. He has known the true day since April 1894, when Mr. Fogg told it to him, and he wrote it that same morning in the margin of his book, in red ink. No man forges a paper with a date which he has himself corrected. Whoever made this form had read the first notebook with great care, and had taken the day from it, and had not troubled to read the margin. You had that notebook for nine weeks."

The editor played for some time with the green pencil. He showed no shame, but rather the air of a man who casts up the loss upon a transaction.

"I have a young man," said he at last, "who is paid to find things. I did not ask him where he found this one."

"I daresay not. Now listen to me. I am not retained by the Post Office to protect its stamps, and I have no wish to see your young man in the dock, still less to see this story tried there, where every word of it would be printed again by your rivals. There are four things which I require. The form which he made, and the block which was cut from it, will be destroyed now, before Mr. Quarmby. The chapter will be printed as the old man wrote it, or not at all. The thirty guineas which are owing to him will go to Lambeth to-night, by hand. And your young man will find other employment. If any one of the four should fail, Mr. Quarmby and I shall meet at Bow Street on Monday, and you may print that."

"You are compounding a felony, Mr. Holmes."

"Very possibly. Is it agreed?"

The editor rang again, gave his orders to the foreman in a few brisk words, and stood by while the metal was broken up. He counted thirty sovereigns and thirty shillings out of a drawer with perfect good humour.

"It is a dull chapter without it," said he, as he sealed the envelope. "An honest man who was wrong! Who on earth will buy that?"

"I have sold several," said the doctor.

As they went down the stairs the machines broke into their full roar. "We go at six with a hole in us," said the editor cheerfully over the banister, "and I shall be obliged to fill the hole with a column upon the Lords!"

It was eight o'clock when they came again to the room off the Kennington Road. The envelope lay unopened upon the mantelpiece, and one glance at the bed was sufficient to show the doctor that his fortnight had been a generous estimate. The old man lay lower upon his pillows, and his breath came with a dry catch in it. He listened with closed eyes while Holmes gave him the history of the afternoon in half a dozen sentences, and when he heard of the five minutes he laughed, once, and paid for it with a long fit of coughing.

"A day too many," he whispered. "I had it in my own margin. I never put it to the train."

"No."

"Then I was wrong again, and it will be printed that I was wrong."

"It will be printed that you were honest."

"It reads the same on a Sunday." He lay for a while without speaking. "And the wreck? You saw him?"

"I saw him. He says that it was four minutes and eleven seconds, and that, if it is corrected, he can have no objection to it."

The old man did not stir. The silence lasted so long that the doctor rose and bent over him, and was met by a pair of eyes which blazed with the first anger that they had shown since the morning.

"Thirty-seven years!" said he. "I have his whole life in a box, and the worst hour of it in my hand to do what I like with, and he corrects my arithmetic!"

"That is what he did."

"Give me that slip, and a pen."

He spread the proof upon the quilt, and across the paragraph which told of the wreck, from the first line of it to the last, he wrote four words, very slowly, and signed his name beneath them. The effort left him grey. It was some minutes before he could speak.

"He gave me eleven minutes once," said he. "I have kept them by me. He can have them back."

"You will have no chapter left."

"I have a man who followed the wrong man round the world. It is what happened." He moved his hand towards the bag. "The books are yours; that was the bargain. Leave them with me to-night. I have an entry to make. And put the one line in, if ever you get it."

"I think that I have it."

"Don't tell me! I shouldn't know what to do with the last seven-and-thirty years."

There was a step upon the stair. It was slow and perfectly even, and it neither paused at the landing nor quickened after it. The old man had turned his head to the door before the others had well heard the sound, and his eyebrows, which had been motionless all day, went up. Mr. Fogg stood upon the threshold with his hat in one hand and his watch in the other. Behind him in the shadow of the landing the doctor could make out the small, upright figure of the lady, who did not come in.

"Seven-and-thirty years," said the old man. "Sit down, Mr. Fogg."

Mr. Fogg looked at his watch. Then he put it in his pocket, and sat.

"I think, Doctor," said Holmes in a low voice, "that this is a point at which a third and a fourth are not wanted."

Upon the pavement they found the steward waiting beside a cab, with a rug over his arm.

"He does not go to his club to-night, monsieur," said he. "He has not said why. I have not asked. It is seven-and-thirty years that I do not ask."

He put the rug about his own shoulders, and settled himself to wait.

The letter reached the farm by the first post of Tuesday, and a large box came with it.

Monsieur,—The old gentleman is dead to-day, Monday, at ten minutes after four in the afternoon. Monsieur was with him on Sunday and on Monday. He did not go to his club on Monday. I have looked for the first time in the book. There is no wager for Monday. There is only the hour.

The landlady says that these books are for you by his wish.

I have left the gas burning in the hall. It is three nights now. I think that I shall send the bill to myself.

Holmes passed the sheet across the breakfast table, opened the box, and found the last of the thirty-seven notebooks lying uppermost. After the entry for the Wednesday there was one more, which straggled badly down the page.

Sat. 18. He came 8h 20m. Stayed.

"Monday was the twentieth," said the doctor, after he had looked at it for some time. "Thirty-seven years to the very day since Liverpool."

"To the true day. He would have been pleased with that. He had it wrong for one-and-twenty of them."

Holmes rose, took down from the shelf the great volume of his index which bore the letter F, and turned over the leaves until he came to an entry of the summer of 1887.

Fogg. Savile Row. Keeps the cable to the minute, for a sovereign, against himself. Why?

He dipped his pen, drew a neat stroke through the last word, and wrote a single line beneath. The doctor read it over his shoulder.

Master of the Sarah Pellew, 1860. Four minutes eleven seconds. Has kept the ship's time since.

"You are not going to send that to him?"

"No. He knows it."

"To her, then?"

"She asked." He returned the volume to its place, gathered the notebooks into their paper, tied the tape about them with the old man's own knots, which he had taken some pains to preserve, and wrote upon the outside the name of the lady and the number in Savile Row.

"And the line which is wanting in the last book?"

"I have left it for the only man who can write it. He has never needed me to tell him the time." Holmes pushed back the curtain and looked out at the white slope of the downs. "The carrier calls at three, Doctor. If you will take one end of this box, we shall have it at the gate before he does; and my housekeeper has a fowl, I understand, which will not keep for a second week-end."
